paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Everyone dreams, usually several times a night, although most dreams are forgotten within minutes of waking. Dreaming mostly occurs during a phase called REM sleep, named after the rapid eye movements that can be seen beneath the eyelids. People woken during REM sleep report vivid, story-like dreams around eighty per cent of the time, compared with about fifteen per cent during other phases.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For centuries, the question of why we dream belonged to philosophers. In the early twentieth century, Sigmund Freud proposed that dreams are disguised expressions of hidden wishes. Few scientists today accept his detailed theories, partly because they cannot be tested. Even so, Freud's idea that dreams are connected to our emotional lives has proved surprisingly durable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Modern research offers three main explanations. The first is that dreaming helps memory. During sleep the brain replays recent experiences and sorts them, strengthening important ones and discarding trivial ones. Students who sleep after studying generally remember more than those who stay awake. The second explanation is emotional: dreams may work like overnight therapy, allowing the brain to process painful experiences without the full chemical response of stress. Brain scans show that during REM sleep the chemical associated with stress is almost absent.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The third theory, proposed by the neuroscientist Antti Revonsuo, suggests that dreams are a kind of simulator. By repeatedly presenting threatening situations, such as being chased, they allow us to rehearse reactions in safety. Evidence for this comes from studies showing that threatening dreams are far more common than pleasant ones across cultures. However, critics point out that many dreams, such as forgetting an exam, involve no physical danger at all.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of these theories excludes the others, and it is possible that dreams serve several purposes at once. What is clear is that disturbing sleep has consequences. People deprived of REM sleep for a few nights become irritable, struggle to concentrate and show poorer memory. The next time a strange dream wakes you, it may be worth remembering that your brain was doing some important work.
